%% ----------------------------------------------------------------------
%% Abstract — written in the thesis voice (formal, third-person,
%% multi-clause). Ends with the three URLs the call for papers requires.
%% ----------------------------------------------------------------------
\begin{abstract}
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software
development workflows, yet a growing body of evidence shows that the code
they generate often contains security vulnerabilities. Prior work has
primarily focused on measuring the prevalence of such issues, providing
useful evidence of risk but limited support for understanding their causes,
tracking how they propagate through development workflows, or integrating
this knowledge into practical security processes.

To address these gaps, we present \textsc{aialib}, an annotated threat
library for AI-generated code. \textsc{aialib} systematically generates,
analyzes, and structures potential vulnerabilities from LLM-produced code, enriching each finding with conventional security taxonomies (CWE and OWASP) together with AI-specific information describing why the vulnerability was generated, how it propagates through code reuse and refactoring, and how it relates to AI-system threat models.


\smallskip\noindent
\textbf{Code and dataset:}
\url{https://github.com/Aljaberi500/aialib}\hfill\\

\url{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20127950}\hfill\\

\url{https://youtu.be/0DpGrvZd8lo}
\end{abstract}

%% ======================================================================
\section{Introduction}
%% ======================================================================

Large language models are now routinely used to write, complete, and
refactor production code, and the empirical literature has shown that the code they emit can contain non-trivial rates of security-sensitive defects~\cite{pearce2022asleep,khoury2023copilot,siddiq2022securityeval}.
This evidence base is dominated by \emph{prevalence} measurements:
counts of insecure completions on fixed benchmarks. Prevalence is
necessary, but it leaves three operational questions unanswered.
\ding{192}~\emph{Why} did the model emit the weakness such as an unsafe default, a
hallucinated dependency, a reused template, a truncated context? \ding{193}~How
does that weakness \emph{propagate} when the snippet is reused or
refactored downstream? \ding{194}~And how does it map onto AI-specific threat
models such as MITRE ATLAS~\cite{mitreatlas}, an adversarial-threat taxonomy for AI systems?

Without structured answers, security teams cannot triage AI-generated
findings differently from classical ones, code-LLM vendors cannot
compare regressions across model versions on a stable protocol, and
CI/CD policies cannot express AI-aware rules such as ``fail the build
if \texttt{unsafe\_default} findings regress''. Detector
tools return CWE~\cite{cwe} labels but no causal
or propagation context; LLM red-team suites target adversarial probing rather than production coding workflows; and
AI-system threat frameworks~\cite{mitreatlas} sit a layer above the
code artifact and are not natively linkable to detector output.

We address this gap with \textsc{aialib}, a
reproducible generation--detection--annotation pipeline alongside the
dataset it produces. The release contributes:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*, topsep=5pt, itemsep=6pt,
                  parsep=0pt, partopsep=0pt]
  \item An \emph{applicable, reproducible pipeline.} A tool that
        generates code from any configured LLM, scans it with two established rule-based static analyzers (Bandit~\cite{bandit}, Semgrep~\cite{semgrep}) plus a custom AI-risk detector, and emits
        annotated findings in a fixed schema. It can be applied to new
        models or new prompts to produce comparable finding sets, used
        to review individual LLM-generated snippets in an IDE-style
        workflow, or re-run deterministically (fixed seed, pinned
        parameters, Docker image) to reproduce our published results.
  \item An \emph{AI-cause vocabulary}: a taxonomy describing why an LLM        generated an insecure construct rather than merely what                vulnerability it contains and \emph{why} a model
        emitted a weakness, not only what the weakness is:
        \path{unsafe_default}, \path{hallucinated_dependency},
        \path{template_reuse}, \path{context_} \path{truncation},
        \path{prompt_misinterpretation}, plus provider-specific
        categories. A curated CWE-to-ATLAS crosswalk connects these
        labels to conventional CWE and OWASP~\cite{owasptop10} tags and to MITRE ATLAS
        techniques, enabling analysis beyond conventional vulnerability classification.
  \item A \emph{504-finding annotated dataset} drawn from 2{,}144
        Python completions across four production LLMs and four
        propagation variants (base, reuse, refactor, secure-refactor),
        exported as CSV, indexed SQLite, and SARIF~\cite{sarif} for direct use in
        CI/CD pipelines and IDE integrations.
  \item \emph{Analyst tooling} for human-in-the-loop review and trust
      calibration, reporting per-rule precision rather than a single
      aggregate number so users of the dataset can weight findings by
      trustworthiness.
\end{enumerate}
The artifact is positioned not as another prevalence study but as a
contribution to AI-aware vulnerability annotation and threat-knowledge
structuring. Its value lies in providing a disciplined way to connect
raw detector outputs to AI-specific causes, propagation labels, and
ATLAS techniques while preserving the provenance required for audit and
re-execution.


%% ======================================================================
\section{Artifact Overview}
%% ======================================================================

\textsc{aialib} is implemented as an offline-first Python~3.11+
pipeline (src/aialib) composed of seven loosely coupled
stages, each invocable as \texttt{python\,-m\,aialib.<stage>} or as a
Make target. Figure~\ref{fig:ai-pipeline} summarizes the data flow from the prompt manifest to the exported library. The design treats prompt
expansion, code generation, scanning, normalization, annotation,
validation, and export as connected parts of a single analytical
chain in which raw outputs, intermediate transformations, and final
annotations remain linked throughout the experiment.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering

\begin{tikzpicture}[font=\small, node distance=6mm]

\node[block] (b1) {\textbf{Prompt Generation}\\[2pt]
Templated, security-relevant prompts\\
(linked to CWEs, difficulty levels)};

\node[block, below=of b1] (b2) {\textbf{LLM Code Generation}\\[2pt]
Multiple LLMs (e.g., GPT-4o, GPT-o4 mini,\\ K2-Think-V2, Sonnet 4.0),\\
multiple samples per prompt};

\node[block, below=of b2] (b3) {\textbf{Static Analysis}\\[2pt]
Bandit, Semgrep;\\
findings normalized to CWE, severity};

\node[block, below=of b3] (b4) {\textbf{AI-Aware Annotation}\\[2pt]
Add AI-Cause, Propagation Vector, Human AI Factor,\\
and ATLAS Technique};

\node[block, below=of b4] (b5) {\textbf{Threat Library Export}\\[2pt]
CSV/SQLite + SARIF for CI/CD};

\draw[line] (b1) -- (b2);
\draw[line] (b2) -- (b3);
\draw[line] (b3) -- (b4);
\draw[line] (b4) -- (b5);


\end{tikzpicture}

\caption{Overview of the methodology used to construct the AI-risk-aware threat library. The pipeline combines prompt generation, multi-LLM code synthesis, static vulnerability analysis, AI-specific threat annotation, and standardized data export.}
\label{fig:ai-pipeline}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Prompt generation framework.} The prompt manifest declares
16 security-relevant template families covering
authentication-related SQL construction, command execution, path
handling, YAML and pickle deserialization, insecure file upload,
secret handling, server-side request forwarding, temporary-file usage,
concurrency, cloud storage access control, XML parsing, and four
AI-specific families that target dependency hallucination, unsafe
defaults, context misalignment, and multi-file output structure. Each
family is parameterized by difficulty levels and stratification caps
that prevent template-rich families from dominating the corpus, and
each is decorated with deterministic mutators that introduce
constraint nudges, ambiguous requirements, and contextual noise. The
final stratified selection contains 134 base prompts, expanded into
four propagation variants: \texttt{base}, \texttt{reuse},
\texttt{refactor}, and \path{secure_refactor}, to yield 536 prompt
instances per provider per run. 

\textbf{Propagation Variants.} The four propagation variants encode different points in the
developer-AI workflow at which insecure code may persist. \emph{Base}
is the prompt as authored, modeling a developer who accepts the first
completion; \emph{reuse} re-frames the same task to model
copy-paste lift of a snippet into a new function context;
\emph{refactor} applies a generic maintenance instruction, modeling
routine cleanup that does not include a security review; and
\emph{secure refactor} explicitly asks the model to harden the
snippet, modeling a security-aware revision pass. The four variants
share a lineage identifier so a given weakness can be tracked across
stages, which is what \path{reports/propagation_report.json}
aggregates as a copy-paste-style proxy for socio-technical
propagation.

\textbf{Template provenance.} The prompt templates were manually
authored by the authors and selected to cover common Python security
weaknesses observed in prior generated-code
studies~\cite{pearce2022asleep,siddiq2022securityeval}, common
CWE/OWASP categories, and AI-specific failure modes such as
dependency hallucination, unsafe defaults, context misalignment, and
multi-file bypasses. Each family is associated with expected sinks
and target CWEs, and stratification caps prevent high-yield families
from dominating the corpus. The full template family-to-CWE table ships with the artifact (\path{docs/template_design.md}).

\textbf{Provider abstraction.} A unified \texttt{Provider} interface
implements deterministic offline generation
(\texttt{LocalGenerator}), and live providers for
OpenAI~(\texttt{gpt-4o-mini}, \texttt{gpt-4.1}),
Anthropic~(\texttt{claude-sonnet-4}), and
MBZUAI-IFM~(\texttt{K2-Think-v2}). Every adapter logs the model
identity, temperature, top-p, maximum token count, system prompt, and
seed alongside each completion so that runs from different providers
remain comparable at the level of input specification and post-generation
processing.

\textbf{Detection and annotation.} Bandit and Semgrep are executed
under vendored rule packs on sandboxed copies of every completion,
and a custom \path{detect_ai_risks} module fires for hallucinated
imports, unsafe defaults such as \texttt{debug=True} and
\texttt{verify=False}, prompt-code misalignment, and multi-file
sanitization bypass patterns. Findings are merged into a canonical
record, decorated with token-level and AST-level fingerprints to
support deduplication and novelty clustering, and passed through a
rule-based annotator that assigns CWE, OWASP, AI-cause, propagation
vector, human-AI factor, and ATLAS technique labels under
\path{configs/annotation_rules.yaml}. A separate ATLAS catalog
constrains the technique vocabulary so that unknown values are
rejected at validation.

\textbf{Rule-based Annotation} Each detector emits a rule identifier, affected code span, sink API, severity, and supporting evidence reference. AIALIB normalizes and deduplicates findings using the completion identifier, sink API, rule identifier, token-level hash, and AST-level hash before passing them to the annotation stage. The annotator consults the detector rule or AI-risk rule defined in \path{configs/annotation_rules.yaml}, which maps findings to CWE, OWASP, AI-cause, propagation vector, human–AI factor, mitigation guidance, and MITRE ATLAS technique identifiers. These annotations represent rule-based inferred classifications derived from static analysis and heuristic matching rather than proven root causes or confirmed exploitability; accordingly, all annotated findings are treated as \path{validation_level = static_only}. A validation gate rejects unknown or inconsistent labels, while the rulebook remains user-configurable, allowing researchers to extend mappings, disable rules, or filter annotations by CWE, severity, AI-cause, or detector.

\textbf{Quality gate, export, and review.} The validation stage
enforces a JSON Schema with twenty-one required fields, checks
rule-mapping coverage, blocks unrecognized severity values, computes
novelty clusters keyed by $(\textit{CWE},\,\textit{sink API},\,\textit{normalized hash})$,
and emits machine-readable reports
(\path{reports/mapping_coverage.json},
\path{reports/novelty_report.json}). Export modules write CSV,
indexed SQLite, and SARIF, the last of which preserves both
conventional security properties and AI-aware metadata for
consumption by IDEs and CI/CD systems. A \texttt{review} package
provides a stratified review queue and a trust-calibration report so
that detector precision can be quantified at the rule level rather
than assumed to be uniform across rules.

\textbf{Reproducibility.} Every run writes
\path{data/run_manifest.json}, recording the random seed, commit
SHA, analyzer versions, ruleset hashes, and pipeline version. A unit
test (\path{tests/}\path{test_expand_deterministic.py})
verifies byte-identical prompt expansion for a fixed seed, and the
same seed is propagated into provider-side generation requests where
supported. Shipped exports are pinned by SHA-256 checksums,
\path{scripts/reproduce_table1.py} recomputes
Table~\ref{tab:providers} from the bundled findings and fails on any
mismatch, and a CI workflow re-runs the unit tests, the validation
gate, and both checks on every push.

\textbf{Environment.} The bundled release was produced on an
x86\_64 host running Ubuntu~24.04.3~LTS with CPython~3.12.3,
glibc~2.39, and GCC~13.3.0, using Bandit~1.7.8 and Semgrep~1.67.0 as
pinned in \path{requirements.txt}. The published Docker image
builds on \path{python:3.11-slim} (Debian~12, Python~3.11,
glibc~2.36) and fixes the reference OS and C library for
re-execution. The manifest carries a dedicated environment block
(host OS, CPU architecture, Python, glibc, and compiler versions),
populated on the executing machine by
\path{scripts/record_env.py}.

\section{The Annotated Threat Library}
%% ======================================================================

The dataset shipped with the artifact
(\path{sample_outputs/threat_library.{csv,sqlite,sarif}})
contains 504 annotated findings drawn from 2{,}144 generated Python
samples (134 base prompts $\times$ 4 propagation variants $\times$ 4
providers). Table~\ref{tab:providers} summarizes the per-provider
yields and severity composition; the full breakdown is included in
\path{sample_outputs/reports/}.

\begin{table}[!htp]
\caption{Per-model results from running the bundled pipeline.
Each model received the same 536 prompts. \textit{HIGH} and \textit{MED} columns refer to the severity of the
\textit{Findings}; no LOW-severity findings were emitted in the bundled
freeze.}
\label{tab:providers}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llrrrrr@{}}
\toprule
Provider & Model  & Findings & Yield & HIGH & MED \\
\midrule
OpenAI    & \texttt{gpt-4o-mini}               & 143 & 0.267 & 47 & 96  \\
OpenAI    & \texttt{gpt-4.1}                   & 142 & 0.265 & 41 & 101 \\
Anthropic & \texttt{claude-sonnet-4}  & 115 & 0.215 & 56 & 59  \\
K2Think   & \texttt{K2-Think-v2}               & 104 & 0.194 & 48 & 56  \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\end{table}

\textbf{Schema.} Each annotated entry conforms to
\path{schemas/threat_ entry.schema.json} and carries twenty-one
required fields. Listing~\ref{lst:schema} reproduces a representative
record. Array fields are serialized as repeated values rather than as
free-form strings so that the library remains queryable from SQL
without additional parsing.



\textbf{Vulnerability profile.} The CWE distribution is concentrated
around a common core (CWE-489, CWE-829, CWE-377, CWE-295, CWE-116,
CWE-20) shared across the OpenAI and K2Think runs, with additional
classes (CWE-502, CWE-78) appearing in the Anthropic run. The
AI-cause distribution is dominated in every run by
\path{unsafe_default}, with \path{hallucinated_dependency}
appearing at exactly twenty-four findings per run and
\path{context_truncation} appearing identically across the OpenAI
and K2Think runs. The Anthropic run additionally exhibits
\path{training_data_gap} and \path{prompt_overfit} categories
under the rulebook, and triggers ATLAS techniques consistent with
data-poisoning and prompt-injection-style behaviors that are absent
from the other runs.

\begin{lstlisting}[style=lstlibrary,caption={Annotated entry excerpt
from \texttt{sample\_outputs/threat\_library.csv}.},label=lst:schema]
vuln_id        : 13dbca45ccbf
language       : python
generator      : openai (gpt-4.1)
prompt_id      : tempfiles_insecure_path_easy_01-refactor
cwe_id         : CWE-377
owasp_tag      : A05:2021-Security Misconfiguration
severity       : MEDIUM
sink_api       : tempfile.mktemp
ai_cause[]            : ["template_reuse"]
propagation_vector[]  : ["filesystem"]
human_ai_factor[]     : ["knowledge_gap"]
atlas_techniques[]    : ["ATLAS:Operational Oversight"]
detection_tools[]     : ["semgrep"]
validation_level      : static_only
mitigation_short      : Prefer NamedTemporaryFile or mkstemp.
normalized_token_hash : 2c5a200d01ba
ast_hash              : ef728aa2521c
review_status         : unreviewed
\end{lstlisting}

\textbf{Coverage and novelty.} Under the freeze used for the bundled
release, the validation gate reports complete rule-to-CWE mapping
coverage and complete ATLAS catalog membership
(\path{reports/mapping_coverage.json}). Novelty analysis groups the
findings into clusters keyed by $(\textit{CWE},\,\textit{sink API},\,\textit{normalized hash})$,
with the large majority of clusters being singletons in the current
freeze (\path{reports/novelty_report.json}).

\textbf{Licensing and access.} Code is released under Apache~2.0; the
threat-library dataset is released under CC~BY~4.0. The repository,
the Zenodo archive, and a Docker image are linked from the abstract.

%% ======================================================================
\section{Usage Scenarios}
%% ======================================================================

\textbf{Scenario A: one-off snippet review.} A developer or
educator places an LLM suggestion into a single file and runs

\begin{lstlisting}[style=lstlibrary,basicstyle=\ttfamily\scriptsize]
python -m aialib.pipeline.process_snippet \
    --code snippet.py \
    --prompt-text "log incoming HTTP body"
\end{lstlisting}

\noindent which writes a self-contained
\path{out/manual_run/threat_library.csv} with the same schema as
the full corpus. This entry point is intended both for IDE-style use
within a code-review workflow and for the \emph{Try it} demonstration
that accompanies the screencast.

\textbf{Scenario B: comparative analysis across providers.}
Researchers can re-run the comparison by altering only the
\texttt{--provider} flag in the orchestration target. Because the
prompt expansion and detector configurations are pinned, any
differences observed in subsequent reports arise from model behavior
under the fixed protocol rather than from changes in prompt content
or analyzer coverage. The bundled
\path{aialib.analysis.compare_providers} module emits
\path{reports/provider_comparison.{json,md}} for direct inclusion
in dashboards or follow-up papers.

\textbf{Scenario C: CI/CD integration.} The SARIF export
(\path{out/threat_library.sarif}) is consumable by GitHub Code
Scanning, GitLab SAST, and most IDE integrations, and preserves
AI-aware properties as structured result metadata. Operators can also
query the SQLite library directly to express AI-cause-aware policies,
for example to fail a build that introduces a regression in the
unsafe-default category:

\begin{lstlisting}[style=lstlibrary,basicstyle=\ttfamily\scriptsize]
SELECT cwe_id, COUNT(*) FROM findings
WHERE "ai_cause[]" LIKE '%unsafe_default%'
  AND severity IN ('HIGH','MEDIUM')
GROUP BY cwe_id;
\end{lstlisting}

%% ======================================================================
\section{Evaluation Evidence}
%% ======================================================================

The artifact has been evaluated along three axes that are treated as
methodological requirements:
\emph{coverage}, \emph{determinism}, and \emph{cross-provider
stability}. Coverage is reported at the validation stage and confirms
that every rule encountered in the bundled freeze is mapped under the
annotation rulebook and that every ATLAS technique label is contained
in the catalog: all 504 entries pass the 21 required field
checks in \path{schemas/}\path{threat_entry.schema.json},
mapping coverage reaches $100\%$ across the three tool sources, and
per-tool and per-rule breakdowns are preserved in
\path{reports/}\path{mapping_coverage.json}.
Determinism is verified by
\texttt{tests/}\path{test_expand_deterministic.py},
which asserts byte-identical prompt expansion under a fixed seed;
combined with provider-side seeding and deterministic fingerprinting,
this allows a clean re-run from the published Docker image to
reproduce the dataset row-for-row. Cross-provider stability is
documented in
\path{reports/}\path{provider_comparison.md}, where
the per-provider yields and severity profiles in
Table~\ref{tab:providers} are reproducible across the same seed; the
report additionally includes a unique-finding column that flags the
K2Think outlier (twenty-one unique patterns on one hundred and four
findings) and motivates the inclusion of multi-provider runs in the
bundled release rather than reliance on a single model.

\subsection{Dataset Composition}

The library's distinguishing dimension is the AI-cause layer:
Table~\ref{tab:ai-cause-distribution} shows its distribution across
the four provider runs. \path{unsafe_default} dominates every run
(229 findings overall); \path{hallucinated_dependency} appears at
exactly twenty-four findings per run, reflecting the fixed
dependency-hallucination prompt budget; and two causes
(\path{training_data_gap}, \path{prompt_overfit}) occur only
in the Anthropic run. Table~\ref{tab:cwe-distribution} gives the
corresponding weakness-class breakdown, and
Table~\ref{tab:providers} the per-provider totals: 504 findings from
2{,}144 completions, 192 HIGH and 312 MEDIUM.

\texttt{hallucinated\_dependency}  & 24 & 24 & 24 & 24 &  96 \\
\texttt{template\_reuse}           & 21 & 32 & 16 & 13 &  82 \\

\texttt{prompt\_misinterpretation} &  7 &  1 &  8 & 11 &  27 \\

\texttt{prompt\_overfit}           &  0 &  0 &  0 &  1 &   1 \\

\texttt{K2-Think-v2}, and \texttt{claude-sonnet-4}.}
\label{tab:ai-cause-distribution}

\subsection{Detector Contribution}

Decomposing the ensemble attributes 406 of the 504 findings
($80.6\%$) to the AI-aware risk detector and the remaining 98
($19.4\%$) to Semgrep; the bundled Bandit rule pack is subsumed by
Semgrep in the present freeze and therefore contributes zero unique
entries, although it is retained in the orchestration so that
independent rule additions remain possible. This breakdown supports
the interpretation that the artifact is dominated by AI-specific risk
classes rather than by re-packaged classical detector output.

\subsection{Evidence Level}

Every entry carries an explicit \path{validation_level} so that
downstream users can distinguish \emph{detected} from
\emph{validated} findings. In the bundled freeze, 229 entries
($45.4\%$) are \path{sandbox_validated}. Their runtime-checkable
signals were confirmed in a sandboxed execution, and the remaining
275 ($54.6\%$) are \path{static_only}, supported by
static-analyzer evidence alone. No entry is yet human-reviewed: the
artifact ships the complete human-in-the-loop pipeline
(\path{aialib.review.queue} for stratified sampling,
\path{aialib.review.apply} for decision merging, and
\path{aialib.analysis.}\path{trust_calibration} for
per-rule precision and disagreement metrics), and per-rule precision
updates incrementally as reviews accumulate, allowing users to
weight findings by rule-level trustworthiness rather than treat them
as uniformly reliable.

\textbf{Limitations.} The current release is intentionally scoped to
Python. Prompt templates, analyzer configurations, fingerprinting
logic, and AI-risk detectors are aligned to that scope, which improves
internal coherence at the cost of language coverage. The
ATLAS-aligned mappings are likewise a curated crosswalk rather than a
formal one-to-one taxonomy, and are documented under
\path{docs/mappings/}. Both restrictions are recorded as v0.2
milestones rather than concealed.

%% ======================================================================
\section{Related Tools and Datasets}
%% ======================================================================

\textsc{aialib} differentiates from prior work along three axes.
Against static benchmarks of vulnerable LLM completions such as
SecurityEval~\cite{siddiq2022securityeval}, the original Copilot
study~\cite{pearce2022asleep}, and the broader empirical literature
on ChatGPT-generated code~\cite{khoury2023copilot}, it ships the
generator alongside the dataset, so the corpus is regrowable as new
LLMs appear and the conditions of generation are auditable rather
than only the snippets. Against detector benchmarks such as
CodeQL~\cite{codeql} and Semgrep rule
suites~\cite{semgrep,bandit}, it adds an AI-cause taxonomy and an
ATLAS-aligned annotation layer rather than a pure CWE label. Against
LLM red-team datasets, including
CyberSecEval~\cite{bhattcybersec2024}, it focuses on production-style
coding prompts under controlled propagation variants making the data usable as a regression
suite for code-completion vendors and CI/CD policy authors.

%% ======================================================================
\section{Availability and Future Work}
%% ======================================================================

The complete artifact, including code, dataset, schemas, configurations,
sample exports, and a Docker image, is released under Apache~2.0
(code) and CC~BY~4.0 (dataset) at
\url{https://github.com/Aljaberi500/aialib}. The v0.1.0 release is
archived on Zenodo at
\url{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20127950}, and a
\texttt{CITATION.cff} is provided for the GitHub citation widget. A screencast walking through Scenarios A--C is at
\url{https://youtu.be/0DpGrvZd8lo}. Planned extensions include
language coverage beyond Python through additional analyzer rule
packs, broader provider coverage as new commercial and open-source
code-LLMs become available, and a hosted threat-library explorer that
allows interactive filtering by CWE, AI-cause, provider, and ATLAS
technique. 

\begin{acks}
This artifact accompanies the master's thesis ``Why AI-Generated Code
Is Vulnerable: Cause Taxonomy, Threat Mapping, and CI/CD Security
Controls'' completed at the Mohamed bin Zayed University of
Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI). The authors thank the Bandit and
Semgrep maintainers for the rule packs that anchor the detector
ensemble and the MITRE ATLAS team for maintaining the technique
catalog.
\end{acks}
